---
title: Comets and asteroids
lang: en
free: true
---
Comets and asteroids are small bodies left over from the formation of the Solar System about 4.6 billion years ago. Although both orbit the Sun and can cross Earth's path, they differ significantly in composition and origin. Comets are icy bodies born in the cold outer reaches of the Solar System — the Kuiper Belt and the distant Oort Cloud — while asteroids are rocky or metallic objects concentrated mainly in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.

When a comet ventures close to the Sun, solar heat vaporises its surface ices, releasing gas and dust that form a glowing coma around the nucleus and one or more tails stretching millions of kilometres. The ion tail always points directly away from the Sun, pushed by the solar wind, while the dust tail curves gently along the orbital path.

## The asteroid belt

The asteroid belt contains millions of rocky fragments ranging from dust-sized grains to Ceres, a dwarf planet nearly 1,000 kilometres in diameter. Jupiter's gravity prevented these bodies from ever coalescing into a full-sized planet. Most asteroids follow stable orbits, but gravitational perturbations occasionally nudge some onto paths that can approach Earth.

## Impacts and science

Asteroid and comet impacts have shaped planetary surfaces throughout Solar System history. Meteorites — fragments that survive the fall to Earth — give scientists pristine samples of early Solar System chemistry, including complex organic molecules that may have seeded life on Earth.
